paragraphs: (a) Rashi, Chullin 44b, says: “Rav Chisda was a priest, as stated in Gittin, HaNizzakin: eighty pairs of priestly brothers married eighty pairs of priestly sisters.” End of quotation. Even if you search with lamps, you will not find this in Gittin, HaNizzakin. Rashi, Shabbat 10b, says Rav Chisda was a priest, as we say concerning a certain town in the Land of Israel containing eighty pairs of priestly brothers married to eighty pairs of sisters: “They searched from Sura to Nehardea, etc.” But the Light of the Exile did not indicate the source's location. See that he forgot its place. Go and you will find it in Berakhot 44a: “There was a town in the Land of Israel called Gofnit, with eighty pairs of priestly brothers married to eighty pairs of priestly sisters. The rabbis searched from Sura to Nehardea and found none except Rav Chisda's daughters, married to Rami and Mar Ukva, sons of Chama. Although the women were of priestly descent, the men were not priests.” End of quotation. In my opinion the Light of the Exile's error in saying “as in Gittin, HaNizzakin” arose because that chapter recounts the destruction. Eikhah Rabbah, on “The Lord swallowed without pity,” says eighty priestly brothers were married to eighty priestly sisters: “In one night they hanged them on one vine,” besides brothers without sisters and sisters without brothers, besides Levites and Israelites. Jerusalem Taanit, chapter 4, halakhah 8, likewise says eighty pairs of priests, etc., married on one night in that Gofna, besides brothers, etc. An erring student wrote in that Rabbah, “In one night they hanged them on one vine.” It is surprising that Mattenot Kehunah did not correct it. The intention is that in a town named Gofna, eighty pairs of priestly brothers married eighty pairs of priestly sisters, besides marriages of brothers without sisters, etc. But neither that Rabbah nor the Jerusalem Talmud mentions Rav Chisda's daughters; only Berakhot above does. I have departed from the bounds of my purpose to bring this matter only incidentally.

(b) He was poor and became wealthy. Tolin, Shabbat 140b: “Neither in my poverty did I eat vegetables, nor in my wealth, etc.” Pesachim 113a: “Had I not brewed beer, I would not have become wealthy.” Bava Kamma 91b: when he walked among thorns and shrubs, he lifted his clothing, saying, “This heals, etc.” Gittin 56a: the rabbis praised Rav Chisda's wood stores. He entrusted all the keys to his attendant except those of the wood, for Rav Chisda said that one storehouse of wheat requires sixty storehouses of wood. Why need it cite Rav Chisda's statement? This is already evident from his not giving his attendant all the keys. One may answer: Yoma, Yom HaKippurim, 75b, says that a kind of quail was supplied to Rav Chisda from heaven among the wood. I might therefore have thought he withheld the wood keys not because of wood's value, but to prevent his attendant taking the quail found among it. It thus brings Rav Chisda's statement to show that he acted because of the wood's importance: Maaseh Tuvyah, in his father's name, 118b.

(c) Mi SheMet, Bava Batra 141a: he said, “For me, daughters are preferable.” Perhaps my sons will become sages, but my daughters will be taken in marriage on account of my honor. Rashbam explains that his sons did not survive. Tosafot rejects this: he had many sons—Rav Nachman, Mar Yenuka, Mar Keshisha, Rav Mari, Rav Pinchas (and Rav Chanan and Rav Tachlifa). Rather, he said daughters were preferable because his sons-in-law were the generation's great men: Rami and Mar Ukva, sons of Chama, and Rava, who married her after Rami died; see there. Afterward he had seven learned sons or more. There were sixty weddings in his household, wealth, and long life; see above. Gilgulei Neshamot (ג״נ), letter alef, writes: Ivtzan is Boaz, who had thirty sons and thirty daughters; all died because he called Manoach a sterile mule. Avdon ben Hillel of Piraton likewise had forty sons and thirty grandsons: they were Rabbah and Rav Chisda, both completely righteous. Rav Chisda's house had sixty weddings; Rabbah's had sixty bereavements. End of quotation. See Moed Katan 28a. He married at sixteen: Kiddushin, chapter 1, 29b, near the end. Rav Chanan bar Rava, Rav's son-in-law, was his father-in-law; see there at length. He chopped beets in honor of the Sabbath: Shabbat 119a. His wife was elderly and adorned herself during the festival. Rav Huna bar Chinena sat before Rav Chisda and said, “They taught this only of a young woman”: Moed Katan 9b. Rav Chisda fasted every Passover eve because he was delicate: if he ate in the morning, the meal would not benefit him—Arvei Pesachim 108. He lived in Kafri: Bava Metzia 6b.

(d) The Chaldean astrologers told him, “You will be a teacher”—you will be a sage: Yevamot 21b. He was so penetrating in reasoning that his colleague Rav Sheshet's whole body trembled from Rav Chisda's reasoning, while Rav Chisda's lips trembled from Rav Sheshet's traditions: Eruvin, chapter 6, 67a. Rav Sheshet was greater than he; see there. Rav Huna told his son Rabbah, “Why are you not regularly before Rav Chisda, whose teachings are sharp?”: Shabbat 82a. The unqualified “judges of Sura” are Rav Huna and Rav Chisda; see there. They are the pious men of Babylonia: Taanit 23b. Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna sat judging all day; Rav Chiyya bar Rav of Difti taught them: Shabbat 10a. See Tosafot, Nazir 27b, which considers and rejects the suggestion that “Rav Chisda’s statement is an invention.” Rabbah bar Rav Huna said: Rav said, etc. Rav Chisda said, “From our teacher's”—Rav's—“words we learn, etc.” R. Nachman said, “Our colleague”—Rav Chisda—“has fallen among great men.” Some say Rabbah bar Rav Huna said, “From our teacher's”—Rav's—“words we learn, etc.” R. Nachman said, “Our colleague's son has fallen among great men.” Rashi explains: Rav Huna was his colleague, and Rabbah his son was “our colleague's son,” since Rav Huna, Rav Chisda, and Rav Nachman were all Rav's students: Beitzah 25a. Bava Metzia 40a, beginning, has “Rabbah likewise said.” Rashi writes that we read Rav: it is not the Gemara's manner to cite amoraim's words in support of a mishnah. Moreover, Rabbah was Rav Chisda's student: how could Rav Chisda speak in his student's name? Rather, we read “Rav likewise said,” Rav being Rav Chisda's teacher. Tosafot writes that we read Rabbah: it is not part of Rav Chisda's speech; the Gemara brings a similar case that came before Rabbah, who ruled like Rav Chisda. End of quotation. But Tosafot, Shabbat 23b, calls Rabbah his colleague. Asheri, Bava Kamma, chapter 5, 49a, says Rav Chisda was greater than Rabbah: Bava Metzia, chapter 1, 6b, R. Oshaya told Rabbah, “When you go before Rav Chisda, ask him.” Rav Chisda expounded in our teacher's name—Rav—and “our teachers who descend from the Land of Israel”—Ulla: Berakhot 38b. Rav Chisda said, “Our great teacher”—Rashi: Rav—“said this, and may the Omnipresent aid him”: Sukkah 33b, near the end, 35b. Niddah 49b has “Rav Chasa said: our great teacher, etc.”; see there. This is a scribal error and should read Rav Chisda. The same matter in Bekhorot 45a has Rav Chisda saying this. Rav's words were dear to him: Shabbat, chapter 1, 10b, he said he would give two gifts to anyone telling him a new teaching in Rav's name. Rava bar Mechasya told him in Rav's name, etc., and he gave him. Arvei Pesachim 107a: he asked Rav; Rav asked R. Chiyya; R. Chiyya asked Rabbi. Eruvin 38b: when Rav died, Rav Chisda entered to raise contradictions between Rav's statements.

(e) Responsa Ralbach, section 126, writes: “You found it difficult that the Jerusalem Talmud says ‘R. Chisda said,’ although he did not live in R. Yochanan's days. This is not so: Rav Chisda did live in R. Yochanan's days, as Raavad's account of tradition explains.” End of quotation. See Yuchasin, after the sequence of amoraim, in their chronological sequence: R. Yochanan died in 4060, and Rav Chisda became head in 4060. See part 1, where you will find one opinion that Rav Chisda died before R. Yochanan. Sefer Keritot says Rav Chisda died in 612, meaning the era of contracts; thus he died in 4060. This requires investigation. Some say he died in 4068; see Rav Huna above. Sheerit Yosef writes that Rav Chisda was R. Yochanan's student. I think this arose because Arvei Pesachim 117a; Yevamot 25b; Nedarim, Naarah HaMeorasah; Bava Batra 120b; Avodah Zarah 27b; Makkot 23a; and the end of Ad Kamma, Bekhorot 31a, have “R. Chisda said: R. Yochanan said.” See the general rules. Yet in my opinion this requires investigation. Kol Shaah, Pesachim 33b: R. Acha son of Rav Avya told Rav Chisda in R. Yochanan's name, and Rav Chisda answered, “Who will heed you and R. Yochanan your teacher?” Nedarim 59a: Rav Chisda told Rava, “Who will heed you and R. Yochanan your teacher?” I think it should read Rabbah, since Rava was not R. Yochanan's student: some say R. Yochanan died before Rav Yehudah, and Rava was born when Rav Yehudah died. I likewise saw in Shevuot 10b that Rav Chisda told Rabbah, “Who will heed you and R. Yochanan your teacher?” I was pleased. Meilah 12a: Rav Chisda told Ulla, “Who will listen to you and R. Yochanan your teacher?” Berakhot 24b: R. Huna said: R. Yochanan said; Rav Chisda told him, “Even if R. Yochanan said it to me with his own mouth, I would not heed him.” But Yevamot says Rabbi received his recompense for not protesting against Avdan, etc., where R. Yishmael son of R. Yosi said, “Is Moses your teacher and not mine?” See there. If R. Yochanan were Rav Chisda's teacher, how could he tell all these men “R. Yochanan your teacher”? He should say “R. Yochanan our teacher.” Furthermore, consider “Even if R. Yochanan said it with his own mouth, I would not heed him”: Tosafot, Eruvin 59b, near the end, says concerning “R. Ammi asked him, etc.” that we do not read “from Rabbah bar Abbahu,” since Rav Nachman would not say “Do not heed him” of his teacher. Menachot 21a: R. Mani asked R. Yochanan about congealed blood, etc. He answered, etc., fell silent, and he said, “Perhaps, etc.” He said, “You reminded me of something R. Chisda said.” Bekhorot 42b in the checked edition: R. Yochanan wondered at one who heeds neither the first tanna nor R. Yishmael. Let R. Yochanan also say, one who heeds not the later rabbis, since Rav Chisda said, “The dispute, etc.” It thus appears that he lived in R. Yochanan's time, but it does not prove he was his student. Tosafot, Bava Metzia 33a, Berakhot 24b, and Shevuot 47b, says Rav Chisda was Rav Huna's student. Zevachim 87: “They say in Rav's school: what is Rav Chisda's reason?” Tosafot writes: “They say in Rav's school” means Rav Huna, and Rav Chisda was his student, etc. We find Rav Huna regularly praising his words: “Your name is Chisda, and your words are gracious”—Gittin, chapter 1, 7a. Rashi there writes Rav Chisda was Rav Huna's student. See Rav Huna the exilarch above: the Jerusalem Talmud has R. Yochanan saying, “Your name is Chisda, and your words are gracious, etc.” Rif, Kol Kitvei and Mefannin, says Rav Chisda was a student before Rav Huna, and the law does not follow a student against his teacher. Yuchasin writes that Rav Chisda was like Rav Huna's student-colleague. Rav Sherira Gaon in Yuchasin likewise calls Rav Chisda Rav Huna's colleague. Tosafot, Eruvin 62b, says Rav Chisda was Rav Huna's student-colleague, and Rav Hamnuna was Rav Chisda's student-colleague; see there, and Rav Huna on the legal decision. Elu Metziot, Bava Metzia 33a: Rav Chisda told Rav Huna, “A student whose teacher needs him ...” Rav Huna answered, “I do not need you. You need me for forty years.” They took offense at one another and stopped visiting each other. Beer Sheva, 52b, writes that a person does not fully grasp his teacher's mind and the wisdom of his teaching until forty years, as in Sifrei, Tavo. Rav Chisda observed forty fasts for distressing Rav Huna; Rav Huna observed forty fasts for suspecting Rav Chisda. Rav Huna asked Rav Chisda: Arvei Pesachim 107a. See Rav Huna as to whether Rav Chisda became academy head after Rav Huna's death or after Rav Yehudah's. He was head at Sura for ten years; see there.

(f) His mouth never ceased studying, and the Angel of Death could not overcome him, until the cedar in the study house split and he stopped studying and died: Makkot 10a; Megallechin. Chiddushei Aggadot writes that he presumably died immediately, but this was not the excision associated with a sudden death, since he was ninety-two years old—Moed Katan 28a—and had reached advanced strength. He died before Rava: Yoma 75b; Tosafot, Yevamot 21b. When he died, they thought to place a Torah scroll on his bier. R. Yitzchak said, etc.; they thought, etc.; R. Yitzchak bar Ammi said, etc.: Moed Katan 25a. When he died, his son R. Yosi spent a night at his grave. He heard rejoicing of groups within the grave: “Let us go to the rejoicing of Rav Chisda's Torah celebration, etc.” They said, “What have the living to do with us, etc.?” He told him, “My son, go away and fulfill your learning. Happy is he who comes here with his learning in hand, for even the ministering angels cannot approach him”: Tziyyoni, Vayechi. See R. Chaggai above. This requires investigation: I have not found that he had a son named R. Yosi.

(g) Sotah 38a, near the end: Rav Chisda said, “We have a tradition: a priest calls out ‘Priests.’” Beer Sheva there writes: “It is puzzling that Jerusalem Talmud, Ein Omdin, has Rav Chisda saying the reverse: the prayer leader must be an Israelite. Perhaps there were two Rav Chisdas. Alternatively, Rav Chisda retracted.” End of quotation. In my opinion, certainly they should initially arrange for the one calling “Priests” to be an Israelite. If no Israelite is there, I might have thought that a priest should not call “Priests,” just as when there is only one priest they do not call “Priests.” He therefore says, “We have a tradition,” that a priest too calls “Priests.” Understand this.
(h) Rav Huna and Rav Chisda: the law follows Rav Huna; see there. I found written: Rav Chisda and Rava, the law follows Rav Chisda. Rav Chisda and Shmuel; see there.

(i) “R. Abba son of Rav Yitzchak said: R. Chisda said.” Abaye told Rav Chisda's interpreter to ask Rav Chisda: Zevachim 14a. Avimi, his teacher. Evyatar sent to him. Rav Oshaya and Rav Chananyah. In R. Acha's name; see there. He sent through Rav Acha son of Rav Huna to Rabbah. Rav Acha bar Rav Yosef—this requires investigation. Rav Acha bar Ulla before him. Rav Acha son of Rav Ulla; see above. Rav Acha bar Azza before him. Rav Acha son of Rav Avya the Elder. Rav Achdevui bar Ammi raised a contradiction for him. Rav Idi, in his name. “Rav Idi bar Avin the carpenter said: R. Chisda said”; Rav Chisda called him “Master.” Rav Chisda said, “I heard it from a great man”—R. Ammi: Yevamot 21b. They brought his ruling before R. Ammi, who challenged it. Later he challenged R. Ammi's words, and they brought it before R. Ammi, etc.; see there. In Ashi's name. A Galilean expounded before him. Rav Dima bar Chinena. Rav Huna, his teacher; see above. Rav Huna bar Rav Katina before him. Rav Huna bar Chinena before him; see above. Rav Hamnuna, student-colleague; see above. Mar Zutra, in his name. “R. Zeira said: R. Chisda said.” “R. Chisda said: R. Zeira said.” “Zeiri said.” In Zeira's name. R. Zeira in R. Chisda's name. R. Chizkiyah, in his name. He asked R. Chizkiyah: Jerusalem Talmud, end of Maaser Sheni and Eglah Arufah. R. Chiyya bar Ashi, in his name. R. Chiyya bar Avin, in his name. R. Chiyya bar Natan, in his name. R. Chiyya bar Avya, in his time. R. Chiyya bar Rav of Difti taught him; see above. R. Chiyya son of Rabbah bar Nachmani, in his name. Rav Chinena Vardan. “R. Chama bar Gurya said.” Rav Chana bar Chanilai. Rav Chanina, in R. Chisda's name: beginning of chapter 1 of Maaserot. Rav Chana bar Rava, his father-in-law. Rav Chanan, his son. Rav Chananyah and R. Oshaya. Rav Chananel. R. Tavi, in his name. “R. Yehudah said.” In R. Yochanan's name; see above. R. Yonah. “R. Yonatan said.” Before R. Yosi. R. Yosah. Rav Yosef called him “Master”: HaZorek, Shabbat 97a, near the end, and 97b, according to Maharshal's reading. Rabbenu Tam's reading reverses this: Rav Chisda called Rav Yosef “Master.” Rav Yeiva the Elder came before him. “R. Yaakov said: R. Chisda said.” R. Yaakov of Adiabene before him. “Rav Chisda said in R. Yitzchak’s name”—Sukkah 44b. R. Yitzchak bar Ammi, his student, was at Rav Chisda's burial; see above. R. Yitzchak bar Shila, his student. “R. Chisda said”—“R. Yirmeyah said”—“Meremar expounded.” “R. Yirmeyah bar Abba said.” Rav Muna. Mar Yenuka and Mar Keshisha, his sons. Rav Mari, his son. In Mari bar Mar's name. Mari bar Isak before him. He said to Mari son of Rav Huna son of R. Yirmeyah bar Abba. “R. Mattana said: R. Chisda said.” Rav Nachman, his son. Rav Nachman, his colleague; see above. “Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: R. Chisda said.” Rav Natan bar Avin, his student. R. Natan bar Abaye before him. Ava before him—this requires investigation. He called Ulla “our teachers”; see above. “Mar Ukva said.” In Mar Ukva bar Chiyya's name. Ravna Ukva. Mar Ukva bar Chama, his son-in-law; see above. Rav Amram, in his name, and he asked him. R. Pinchas, his son. Rav Pappa bar Shmuel—this requires investigation. Rav Pappa, in his name. “R. Katina said.” Rav, his teacher; see above. Rava, his son-in-law and student, called Rav Chisda “old man”: Niddah 61b. He prayed to be given Rav Chisda's wealth, and it was given him. Rabbah, his student or colleague; see above. Rabbah told him, “We expound in your name, etc.” He answered, “May it be His will that you expound all such excellent matters in my name”: Beitzah 28a, near the end. Rabbah bar Shmuel objected to him. He said to Rabbah bar bar Chana. Rabbah bar Rav Huna; see above. Rabbah bar Shila, in his time. Ravin bar Chinena before him. “Ravina bar Shila said.” Rami bar Chama, his son-in-law, asked him. Rami bar Abba. Rami bar Temari said to him. Rafram bar Pappa. R. Shabbetai: Jerusalem Talmud, HaShutafin SheNaderu. “R. Shizvi said: R. Chisda said.” R. Shizvi bar Yeimar said to him. Rav Shila said to him. Rav Sheshet asked him, and he asked Rav Sheshet: HaDar, Eruvin 67a. Rav Tachlifa, his son. Rav Tachlifa of the West. Rav Tachlifa bar Avdimi said to him.
